summary: Revises the FTP reply codes, updating RFC 542. Reply codes are the numeric responses a file transfer server sends to indicate success, failure or progress.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC revises FTP reply codes so programs can identify command results from the numeric code. It also changes when the preliminary reply for a file transfer is sent.

questions: what changed in ftp reply codes
what do the digits in an ftp reply code mean
what is a multi-line ftp reply
how do 4yz and 5yz ftp replies differ
subtitle: A revised three-digit FTP reply scheme for programs and users.

tldr.problem: FTP user processes needed to determine command results from reply codes without relying on server-specific reply text.
tldr.mechanism: The first digit indicates the general result, the second groups its subject and the third gives a more specific meaning.
tldr.outcome: RFC 640 modifies RFC 542. Together, they define the FTP implementation associated with socket 21.

today: RFC 640 has status listed as Unknown and updates RFC 542. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 640.

sections.title: Purpose and Transfer Reply Timing
sections.content:
The revision aims to let a user protocol interpreter determine the outcome of each command by examining the first digit of the reply code. The text after the code is intended for a human user and may vary by server.

For transfer commands, the preliminary reply now indicates that the file can be transferred and that the data connection already exists or an attempt to establish it is about to begin. Earlier specifications sent that reply after establishing the connection, which caused difficulty for interpreters monitoring two connections asynchronously.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can use the first reply digit to decide whether a command succeeded, failed or needs more information. For a transfer, the preliminary reply comes before or as the data connection is being established.

sections.title: Reply Format and Multiple Lines
sections.content:
An FTP reply is a three-digit code followed by a space, text and the Telnet end-of-line code. The code is for a user process; the text is for a person. The code should contain enough information that the process does not need to examine the text.

A multi-line reply begins with the code followed by a hyphen. Its last line begins with the same code followed by a space. The process can detect the end by looking for that code and space at the start of a line. Multi-line replies are not nested; system messages do not carry reply codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A reply has a numeric code and explanatory text. For a multi-line reply, the same code marks the beginning and end.

sections.title: Meaning of the Digits
sections.content:
The first digit classifies the result. A 1yz reply is positive preliminary, 2yz positive completion, 3yz positive intermediate, 4yz transient negative completion, and 5yz permanent negative completion. A 4yz result may be retried without changing the request; a 5yz result discourages repeating the exact request.

The second digit groups the subject: x0z syntax, x1z information, x2z connections, x3z authentication and accounting, x4z unspecified, and x5z file system. The third digit gives a finer meaning within the group.
sections.plainLanguage: The first digit tells whether the action is starting, complete, waiting for more information, temporarily unsuccessful or unsuccessful without an unchanged retry. The other digits narrow down the reply's subject and meaning.

sections.title: Examples and Command Sequences
sections.content:
The RFC lists specific replies such as 200 for a command that is okay, 331 for a request for a password, 425 when a data connection cannot open, and 550 when a requested file is unavailable. The text is suggestive, but servers should follow the defined codes rather than inventing codes for slightly different situations.

The document also lists possible replies for command groups and includes state diagrams. It says a 202 positive completion reply can let a simple user process proceed when a command is irrelevant at a particular site.
sections.plainLanguage: Each listed code has a defined use, such as asking for a password or reporting an unavailable file. The RFC also shows replies expected for command sequences.

viz.caption: FIRST DIGIT OF AN FTP REPLY

items.label: Positive Preliminary
items.desc: Action is starting; expect another reply.

items.label: Positive Intermediate
items.desc: The command was accepted; further information is needed.

items.label: Transient Negative
items.desc: The action failed temporarily and may be requested again.

items.label: Permanent Negative
items.desc: The action failed; do not repeat the exact request.

references.text: RFC 542, File Transfer Protocol, whose protocol RFC 640 modifies.
